public_rationale: Marcus's explicit chronological point holds: broad regulation of general-purpose AI was not first proposed at the last minute in December 2023. The French Presidency's May 13, 2022 text already proposed duties and exemptions. This supports his stated last-minute reading. It does not establish that every final foundation-model obligation existed then, or that LeCun's full statement was knowingly false.
limitations: The result depends on Marcus's explicit interpretation of late as last-minute.
The cited text is a negotiating proposal, not enacted law.
General-purpose AI provisions in 2022 do not establish the introduction dates of all later model-specific provisions.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Claiming that foundation model regulation was added late to the EU AI Act text is a major misrepresentation.

statement.excerpt: The phrase “Added late in the text” — which tries to paint the regulation of foundation models as some kind of sneaky last minute move — is a massive, massive misrepresentation.
statement.document_title: Meta’s Chief AI Officer is lying about the EU AI Act

from_speaker: some kind of sneaky last minute move
our_interpretation: Marcus explicitly explains late as a last-minute addition around the December 2023 agreement. The testable core is whether broad general-purpose AI regulation had appeared substantially earlier.
The target period covers the legislative process from the April 2021 proposal through the December 12, 2023 post.
Following Marcus's stated scope, general-purpose AI provisions count as relevant predecessors to foundation-model regulation. They need not contain every obligation in the eventual agreement.
The assessment concerns chronology, not whether LeCun intended to deceive or whether massive is a measurable degree of error.
criteria.support_condition: Dated negotiating texts contain substantive proposed requirements for general-purpose AI well before the final December 2023 negotiations.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The relevant broad regulatory provisions first appeared only during the final December negotiations, with earlier texts containing no substantive proposed duties.

evidence.excerpt:
Requirements and obligations for general purpose AI systems laid down in Article 4b
shall not apply to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.
evidence.locator: Council document 9029/22, page 7, proposed Article 55a(3); related duties in Article 4b on page 5
evidence.publisher: Council of the European Union, French Presidency; copy hosted by the Future of Life Institute
evidence.explanation: The May 2022 proposal contains general-purpose AI duties in Article 4b and expressly exempts smaller enterprises from them. Proposed regulation therefore existed well before December 2023, although this does not date every provision in the eventual agreement.
